title: Income Management
summary: Family income is the money, goods and services available to the family to fulfil its needs and desires: money income (salary, business, rent, interest, household production sold) plus real income (goods and services enjoyed: free house or car from the employer, kitchen garden produce, doing chores or stitching clothes yourself, caring for equipment). Family income = money income + real income. Needs (basic: food, clothing and shelter; secondary: transport, education, entertainment) must be met first; then desires: comforts (cooler, fan) and luxuries (air-conditioner).

Expenditure is the money spent on goods and services. A spending plan divides money income among food, clothing, housing, education, transport, services, entertainment and savings; primary needs come first, then secondary needs, then desires (comforts before luxuries); each area must last the full month; keep expenditure less than income to save. Income management is the planned and controlled use of family income: planning (including savings) and controlling (avoid waste, buy from cooperative stores or wholesale markets, use time, energy and skill to cut costs: real income). There is no ready-made plan, because families with the same income have different needs.

A record has date, income, item purchased, quantity, rate, amount spent and balance (balance = previous balance − the day's expenses; e.g. Rs 5,000 − 478 = Rs 4,522). Advantages: shows exactly how much is spent and on what, checks unnecessary spending, compares months, helps plan the future and shows market trends.

Income generating activities (pickles, jams, stitching, knitting, toys, tuition), part-time jobs, investing savings to earn interest, wise use of resources (renting part of a house, lending a tractor) and cutting expenditure (doing cleaning or ironing yourself): 'money saved is money earned'.

Savings are the part of present income put aside for emergency or future use. Reasons: a secure future after retirement, emergencies (illness, accident), family goals (house, car), raising the standard of living (washing machine; or buy on instalments), and starting a small business. Guidelines: a realistic plan, a regular plan and a clear purpose. Investment means making savings grow (money kept at home does not grow, can be stolen and tempts spending). Financial institutions keep money safe, pay interest, allow withdrawal and give loans.

Avenues: Bank (safe, interest, withdrawal, loan against fixed deposit; savings account needs a form, signature, two photographs and an introducer; pass book, cheque book and nominee). Post office (convenient, start with Rs 20, tax-free interest in schemes like NSC and Indira Vikas Patra, rebate). Provident Fund (compulsory saving; GPF for salaried, PPF for the self-employed through the SBI or post office; interest and deposits exempt from tax; loan facility). Insurance (general insurance against theft, fire or flood, one-year contract; life insurance: premium, money with interest returned or paid to the nominee/beneficiary on death, tax relief, forced saving). UTI (units of face value Rs 10, minimum 100, dividends exempt from tax, can be encashed, safe). Shares (part ownership, share profit and loss, high return but risky, depends on the Sensex). Debentures or bonds (a loan to the company with fixed interest irrespective of profit; safer than shares). Property or jewellery (can pledge for loans but selling may take time or lose weight). Table of characteristics: savings bank account, post office savings account and units offer liquidity; NSC, GPF, PPF, life insurance and units give tax benefits; GPF, PPF and life insurance offer loan facility.

Selecting an investment: capacity to save, safety, higher rate of interest, easy liquidity, other benefits (dividends, tax relief), purchasing power (return should exceed inflation) and convenient place. Other facilities: credit card (plastic money; high interest on outstanding balance), debit card (issued against a savings account and debited automatically), ATM card (24-hour cash), loans (personal, education, house and vehicle; against a guarantee, bond or security) and e-banking (balance, bills, tickets, payments through the internet).

objective: Identify the activities as Money Income (MI), Real Income (RI), Need (N) or Desire (D). (i) Getting free petrol allowance from the company (ii) Purchasing a new video game (iii) Interest received from a fixed deposit (iv) Purchasing medicines during illness.
(i) Real income (RI). (ii) Desire (D). (iii) Money income (MI). (iv) Need (N).
Mention four investment schemes which offer liquidity.
Savings bank account, post office savings account, units of UTI and gold or property (which can be sold).
Write any four advantages of saving.
A secure future after retirement, meeting emergencies, fulfilling family goals and raising the standard of living (or starting a small business).
Match Column A with Column B. A: (a) General Provident Fund (b) Debentures. B: (i) Loan to a company at fixed interest (ii) Compulsory saving for salaried employees (iii) Part ownership of a company.
State True or False. (a) Making pickles for your family is real income. (b) Income management is useful only when income is large.
(a) True. (b) False: it is needed at every income level.
vsa: Ritu sells pickles to support her family and has also kept a paying guest. Identify this income and give two suggestions to increase it.
This is money income from an income generating activity and from renting part of the house. She can take bulk orders and sell through shops, and use the spare room for more paying guests.

or: Ravi grows his own vegetables behind his house and uses public transport. Identify these incomes and give two suggestions to increase them.
Growing vegetables is real income (goods) and using public transport saves money, also a real income. He can grow more vegetables and use the surplus and share transport or walk for short trips.

vsa: What is meant by income management? Name its steps.
It is the planned and controlled use of the family income. The steps are planning the use of income with savings and controlling the expenditure.
List two advantages of keeping money in a post office.
Post offices are conveniently located and an account can be started with a very small amount. Interest in many schemes is exempt from income tax.
Needs are requirements that must be met, such as food, clothing and shelter. Desires are things we wish to have but which are not necessary for life.
What is meant by supplementing family income? Give two ways.
It means adding to the regular income. Examples are an income generating activity at home and a part-time job.
sa: Explain the guidelines for preparing an expenditure plan (three points).

(i) Divide the money income among areas such as food, clothing, housing, education and savings. (ii) Meet primary needs first, then secondary needs, then comforts and luxuries. (iii) Keep enough for each area for the full month and keep expenditure below income so that savings are possible.
Explain the advantages of maintaining a record of income and expenditure (three points).

(i) It shows exactly how much is spent and on what. (ii) It checks unnecessary spending and allows comparison of different months. (iii) It helps in future planning and shows market trends through the rate column.
Explain the factors to be considered while selecting an investment scheme (three points).
(i) Capacity to save, safety and a higher rate of interest. (ii) Easy liquidity and other benefits such as tax relief. (iii) Purchasing power above inflation and a convenient place.
la: Explain any five investment avenues with their advantages.

(i) Bank: safe, interest, withdrawal and loans against fixed deposits. (ii) Post office: convenient, small amounts, tax-free interest in NSC. (iii) Provident Fund: compulsory saving, tax exemption and loans (GPF and PPF). (iv) Life insurance: safe, financial protection for dependents, tax relief and forced saving. (v) UTI units: regular dividend, tax relief and can be encashed. (vi) Shares and debentures: shares give possible high returns with risk; debentures give a fixed interest with more safety.
